newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FEATURE - Time might finally be right for oil shale.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Time might finally be right for oil shale.

text.p: Central Pacific Minerals NL and Southern Pacific Petroleum NL are closer now than anytime in the last 20 years to starting the A$3 billion (US$2.28 billion) Stuart oil shale project in central Queensland.
Subject to completion of funding arrangements, construction of a A$250 million demonstration plant is expected to begin "in the coming weeks," a Southern Pacific spokesman told Reuters.
The long-time partners have access to a staggering amount of oil -- 25.5 billion barrels in 10 deposits.
Indeed, analysts believe the start of stage one of the Stuart project may well lead to many countries thinking about their own remaining oil reserves and how they might be supplemented.

What has excited international investors and some oil producers faced with declining reserves is that the Stuart resource is 10 times greater than Australia's current proved reserves of conventional oil. It is also more than the total proven oil reserves in the United States and almost twice those of Britain.
STUART COULD BECOME A WORLD-RANKED OIL REGION

Discovered by the two companies during the 1970s, the zone of oil shale along Queensland's coast comprises a total resource of more than 28 billion barrels which may ultimately be ranked as one of the most oil productive regions in the world, Brisbane-based brokerage firm Wilson HTM said in a report.
The find coincided with the rise in world oil prices in the late 1970s and a worldwide interest in synthetic fuels.

In 1980, Exxon Corp, attracted by the relative superiority of the Queensland reserves, entered a 50-50 joint venture with the two companies. A few years later, Exxon ended its involvement as oil prices started to fall and studies showed how capital intensive a large-scale oil shale development would be.
Since then, new technology has been developed and mining and production processes significantly improved, Wilson HTM analysts said.
"Capital costs are now substantially reduced and operating costs more than halved," they said.
OTHER COUNTRIES HAVE PROJECTS UNDERWAY
Oil shale, a sedimentary rock containing a solid hydrocarbon, is the first stage of the formation of oil and gas fields, Southern Pacific explained in its annual report.
The process of extracting oil from oil shale had been known for centuries with the first significant commercial development in Scotland in the 1850s.
Apart from Australia, the overseas focus on oil shale has been on deposits in Estonia, Brazil, the United States, Canada and China.
Southern Pacific said oil shale production in Estonia was well-established but used mostly as fuel for two of its major power stations.
Brazil was carrying out research aimed at producing 3,500 barrels a day. United States oil shale centred in the Colorado region of the Rocky Mountains but this was not economic at current oil prices.
CANADA'S SUNCORP HAS BECOME A PARTNER
The companies and Canadian oil sands producer Suncor Energy Inc, which has agreed to commit to half of the project, plan to produce the Stuart field's first commercial oil in the first half of 1999.

Wilson HTM said Suncor is an experienced operator of mega-projects. The Canadian oil sands industry currently produces more than 270,000 barrels of oil a day, representing about 20 percent of Canada's total consumption.
Both Suncor and Syncrude Canada Ltd operate two synthetic crude plants extracting oil sands using open-cut mining techniques.
Suncor's project at Fort McMurray in northern Alberta is one of the biggest open-cut mining operations in the world and is directly comparable in size to Stuart stage three, Wilson HTM said.
Suncor mines about 80 million tonnes annually to produce 77,600 barrels of oil per day.
This compares with 72 million tonnes of material annually for Stuart Stage Three and a daily production rate of 65,000 barrels.
AUSTRALIA MIGHT HAVE A WHOLE NEW INDUSTRY
"Succesful development of Stuart combined with several factors provide the ingredient for a major shale oil industry in eastern Australia," said Wilson HTM's report.

Wilson's analysts underlined the size of the resource with potential for 50 years of oil production as well as favourable climate, ports and mining infrastructure in place and the strong links with Suncor and its technological expertise.
Total production from the first three stages of Stuart is estimated at 30.7 million barrels a year.
Full development of Stuart will ultimately reach more than 70 million barrels a year at full production.
